items.questionAndWhy: Does reliance on AI relate to subsequent critical-thinking disposition among future teachers, and do AI self-efficacy and stress change that relationship? The distinction matters when evaluating whether AI-assisted work develops independent judgment or merely completes assignments.
items.whatTheyDid: A peer-reviewed longitudinal survey tracked 461 pre-service teachers in Jiangxi, China, through three measurement phases. Researchers modeled reported AI dependence, AI self-efficacy, perceived stress and critical-thinking disposition using structural-equation mediation and moderation analyses.
items.whatTheyFound: Greater reported AI dependence negatively predicted critical-thinking disposition. AI self-efficacy statistically mediated part of this relationship, and the dependence–self-efficacy association was more negative at higher perceived stress. The proposed second-stage moderation was not significant. Although temporally repeated, self-report and unmeasured confounding prevent a definitive causal claim.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX practitioner education and AI-assisted analysis, measure independent reasoning, tool-use patterns, AI self-efficacy and workload separately. A randomized training design could test whether scaffolded AI use preserves independent judgment. These observational teacher-training relationships do not establish that using AI causes critical-thinking decline in analysts.
items.streamTitle: AI dependence predicted lower critical-thinking disposition across three teacher-training waves
items.streamSummary: A three-wave study of 461 Chinese pre-service teachers associated greater AI dependence with lower critical-thinking disposition; AI self-efficacy partially mediated and stress moderated one path. Observational associations are not causal effects.
items.attribution: Zhu, Yang, Long et al. — Scientific Reports (three-wave longitudinal survey; November 17, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can a single visible facial characteristic influence young children's stated friendship preferences, and does the preference vary across types of appearance change? The study examines the emergence of social evaluations early in childhood.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers recruited 139 children aged three to seven from two Hungarian kindergartens. Each child completed 12 paired choices between digitally altered photos of the same face showing healthy, fractured, missing or carious front teeth; trial-level decisions were analyzed with a mixed-effects Bradley–Terry model.
items.whatTheyFound: Children favored healthy dentition, followed by fractured, missing and carious teeth. All pairwise contrasts remained significant after Holm correction (p<0.001); some age and sex differences emerged. Participants made hypothetical image-based choices, not observed friendships, and the limited kindergarten sample restricts generalization.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX social-perception research, this is evidence that incidental visible cues can influence early social-selection judgments even when identity is held constant. The transferable experimental principle is to isolate appearance cues from other characteristics. It does not demonstrate discrimination in real peer networks or analogous judgments in adult political audiences.
items.streamTitle: Preschool children showed appearance-based peer preferences in controlled comparisons
items.streamSummary: In 139 children aged three to seven, controlled same-face image comparisons showed graded hypothetical peer preferences by visible dental condition. The result measures immediate appearance-based judgments, not actual friendships.
items.attribution: Benke, Zsido, Basler et al. — Scientific Reports (preschool choice experiment; November 17, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: What biological process contributes to the loss of a motor skill after it has been learned? Forgetting may involve active remodeling rather than only passive fading of a memory trace.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers used mouse motor-learning tasks, activity labeling, microscopy and genetic manipulation of the CD47 'don't eat me' signal on memory-associated oligodendrocytes. They examined whether microglia removed myelin sheaths associated with previously active motor-memory circuits.
items.whatTheyFound: Reduced motor-engram activity lowered oligodendrocyte CD47 signaling, increased microglial engulfment of learning-associated myelin and accompanied memory decline. Targeted CD47 deletion accelerated myelin loss and motor-memory decay, whereas increased CD47 had opposing effects. These are mechanistic animal experiments, not tests of human memory interventions.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX behavioral science and training research, this provides a biological reminder that retaining a learned response can involve processes distinct from initial acquisition. It does not establish a method to prevent human skill loss or explain forgetting of narratives, beliefs or analyst procedures; those extensions require human evidence.
items.streamTitle: Mouse experiments linked motor-memory decay to removal of learning-associated myelin
items.streamSummary: Mouse experiments showed microglial removal of motor-learning-associated myelin contributes to memory decay, with CD47 manipulation changing decay. Generalization to human knowledge or training retention is untested.
items.attribution: Hu, Luo, Zhou et al. — Nature Neuroscience (mouse causal neurobiology experiments; November 17, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: What organizational and decision-making weaknesses might constrain China's military performance despite major equipment modernization, and how should planners distinguish observable capacity from wartime effectiveness?
items.whatTheyDid: A November 16 CSIS report synthesized historical and contemporary military evidence and extensive interviews with military operators from the United States, Japan, Australia, India, the Philippines and other countries with direct experience of the PLA. It examined command, joint operations, dynamic targeting, logistics, power projection, corruption and the absence of major combat since 1979.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors judge that PLA operational effectiveness may be constrained by centralized command, insufficient combat experience, integration and logistical problems, and institutional corruption. They propose cost-imposing allied deterrence options. These are analyst assessments and recommendations, not observed outcomes of a contemporary PLA war or a controlled organizational comparison.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX operational scenario development, distinguish platforms and force size from the decisions, information flows and learning behaviors required to employ them. Treat command flexibility, targeting coordination and adaptation as uncertain variables to test in wargames, not established incapacity or guaranteed avenues of deterrence.
items.streamTitle: CSIS assessed PLA mission-command and joint-warfighting vulnerabilities behind modernization
items.streamSummary: A November 16 CSIS report argues that PLA modernization may mask vulnerabilities in command, joint operations, logistics, dynamic targeting and corruption. It is interview-informed operational assessment, not measured wartime performance.
items.attribution: Jones, Heginbotham and Byman — CSIS, Peace Disease: Is the PLA Battle Ready? (research report; November 16, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can language models substitute for or supplement representative human surveys, and does generating demographic personas improve estimates of actual public opinion?
items.whatTheyDid: Across three studies, researchers compared GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o variants and Llama 3.3 with published Pew Research Center response distributions. They assessed aggregate prediction, simulated individual personas, model and topic variation, and prompt-context sensitivity against statistical and historical baselines.
items.whatTheyFound: GPT-4's aggregate estimates achieved mean absolute errors around 4–8.5% in reported comparisons, often better than tested simple baselines. But models underrepresented Republican positions, understated uncertainty and sometimes generated overly homogeneous responses. Aggregating persona-generated individuals was less accurate than asking directly for aggregate distributions. No new representative human survey was conducted.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX synthetic audiences, compare generated response distributions with held-out human polling by subgroup, question and uncertainty rather than judging face-validity of individual personas. Models may support exploratory scenario hypotheses but are not substitutes for representative measurement; performance cannot be assumed outside surveyed topics.
items.streamTitle: LLM public-opinion estimates approximated aggregate surveys but distorted partisan distributions
items.streamSummary: Three studies benchmarked LLM estimates against Pew polling: some aggregate estimates approached survey distributions, but partisan bias, excessive homogeneity and inferior persona-aggregation threatened validity. LLM answers are not human survey observations.
items.attribution: Li, Wang, Xie et al. — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (public-opinion benchmarking; November 17, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can AI agents be induced to accept an unsupported claim even when every presented source fragment is individually truthful? The failure occurs when a plausible relationship inferred between facts is mistaken for direct evidence.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers constructed Generative Montage to arrange factual fragments into misleading narratives across 1,090 rumor targets from six Twitter events. They evaluated 14 language models, reviewed multi-agent voting and evidence inspection, and prototyped Grounded Monitor to check whether individual relationships had direct support.
items.whatTheyFound: Overall rumor acceptance exceeded 65% in 12 of 14 models, and remained above 50% under tested majority-vote or same-evidence review conditions. Direct-support monitoring improved judgment accuracy by 5.6–29.0 percentage points. The experiments concern AI agents under designed prompts, not observed acceptance by human audiences.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX AI research and cognitive-security workflows, verify not only each source claim but also the inferred relationships linking claims to a conclusion. Independent evidence of a connection matters more than repeating internally consistent summaries. Applying these AI-agent failure rates to human rumor belief would be invalid.
items.streamTitle: Truthful fragments misled AI agents into unsupported narratives across rumor events
items.streamSummary: Across 1,090 rumor targets, AI agents often accepted misleading narratives assembled from truthful facts; checking direct support for inferred links improved accuracy. These are synthetic-agent findings, not human persuasion rates.
items.attribution: Hu, He, Huang et al. — arXiv preprint, Generative Montage (AI-agent narrative-evidence evaluation; November 16, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can AI-generated video be detected using traces of how it was generated rather than visible defects that newer systems can conceal?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers studied a periodic reconstruction-error pattern arising from temporal grouping in video variational autoencoders. They tested 39 variants of 31 generators, including closed-source systems, and evaluated a training-free phase scan, its integration into existing detectors and a learned detector called CaDet on video-forensics benchmarks.
items.whatTheyFound: The proposed rhythm appeared in many tested video generators. The training-free score beat 15 retrained baselines on DF26; adding it improved 19 tested detectors by 6.7–23.7 percentage points in AUROC, and a CaDet variant trained without generated videos exceeded 90% AUROC on AIGVDBench. These are preprint benchmark results; camera pipelines, editing, new generators and adversarial countermeasures could change field error rates.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX cognitive-security tooling, generation-process traces may complement provenance metadata and perceptual forensics. Before deployment, measure false positives and robustness to real-world editing and new video generators; detecting synthesis is not equivalent to proving a clip is deceptive or measuring audience effects.
items.streamTitle: Video-detector research found periodic decoding signatures in many generated clips
items.streamSummary: A November 16 preprint detected periodic video-decoder traces across many generators and improved benchmark detector AUROC. The results concern synthetic-video classification, not verified operational detection or reduced influence.
items.attribution: Sun, Li, Mei and Shou — arXiv preprint, VAE Rhythm (generated-video forensics benchmark; November 16, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can social-influence models infer peer effects when the analyst knows an individual's contacts but does not observe which contact they actually attended to or whether they ignored that contact?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers introduced a probabilistic agent-based opinion model with two unobserved mechanisms: selection of one encountered neighbor and retention or rejection of the encountered opinion. They developed maximum-likelihood estimation from opinion trajectories and tested synthetic cases plus 15 empirical social-influence datasets.
items.whatTheyFound: Accounting for unobserved attention increased held-out predictive likelihood in 14 of 15 datasets. Synthetic comparisons showed omitting selection or retention could underestimate the magnitude and obscure the shape of influence interactions. Predictive improvement does not identify exactly who saw whom or establish causal exposure effects without further data.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX FCM/ABM research, separate nominal network ties from effective exposure and adoption. Sensitivity tests can compare attention and rejection rules when contact traces are missing. This older October methodology is included because it directly addresses a recurring model-identification problem; forecasts of intervention effects remain unvalidated.
items.streamTitle: Latent attention improved prediction of social influence in 14 of 15 datasets
items.streamSummary: A probabilistic social-influence model added unobserved neighbor selection and opinion retention, improving held-out likelihood on 14 of 15 empirical datasets. Better fit does not by itself identify causal influence.
items.attribution: Thompson, Tian, Huynh et al. — arXiv preprint, Learning Social Influence with Unobserved Attention (methods and empirical evaluation; October 8, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can time-ordered, continuously evolving data reveal more about causal structure when some common causes remain hidden, without relying on conditional independences that cannot be tested?
items.whatTheyDid: A November 16 methods preprint introduced W-separation for directed mixed graphs representing continuous-time stochastic processes. The authors proved a global Markov property for a class of stochastic differential equations and characterized equivalent graph structures with a unique greatest representative.
items.whatTheyFound: The mathematical results provide conditions under which differently oriented or confounded graphs entail the same testable time-series independence model. They also specify permissible edge additions within an equivalence class. The paper presents formal theory, not an empirical demonstration of a human behavioral causal graph or predictive intervention accuracy.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX temporal causal modeling, it provides a candidate way to report which directions are identifiable and which remain observationally equivalent when latent causes exist. A transfer to time-stamped social interaction data is a methodological hypothesis requiring adequate sampling, assumption checking and prospective validation.
items.streamTitle: Continuous-time causal-graph theory characterized what can be learned under latent confounding
items.streamSummary: W-separation yields formal, testable equivalence classes for continuous-time causal graphs with hidden common causes. It advances identification theory but supplies no validated human intervention forecasts.
items.attribution: Kempf, Kilbertus and Manten — arXiv preprint (continuous-time causal-discovery theory; November 16, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can public survey and census data be combined into reproducible, geographically detailed synthetic populations that preserve relationships among multiple attributes rather than generating independent demographic averages?
items.whatTheyDid: The SHAPE project released 2024 U.S. county- and census-tract-level synthetic population estimates built using hierarchical iterative proportional fitting, public survey and census inputs, open code and a GIS dashboard. Outputs cover seven sociodemographic variables, two health behaviors and eleven health outcomes; 2023 estimates were compared with CDC PLACES.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors report strong overall agreement with external small-area public-health estimates, varying by outcome and geography. This is a dataset and methodological validation in public-health characteristics, not an observed model of political attitudes or intervention responses.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX audience modeling, the specific transferable method is constrained small-area synthetic population construction that preserves joint attributes and exposes geographic uncertainty. Reusing the SHAPE workflow with validated behavioral covariates is an untested proposal; health outcome profiles must not be treated as proxies for influence susceptibility.
items.streamTitle: Open tract-level synthetic populations preserve demographic–health joint structure
items.streamSummary: SHAPE released open 2024 U.S. tract/county synthetic populations and validated health-related small-area estimates against CDC data. It is a reproducible population-data infrastructure, not a behavioral influence prediction model.
items.attribution: Von Hoene, Gupta, Von Hoene et al. — Scientific Data (SHAPE public dataset and GIS tools; November 17, 2026)
